originalGroup.material:
Learning the laundry room

For many students, moving into accommodation means learning to use unfamiliar washing ____1____. At home, somebody else may have selected a programme or dealt with a leaking pipe. In a ____2____ laundry room, personal habits also affect the people who use the space next.

Start by checking the small ____3____ sewn into your clothes. These may specify temperatures or warn against a particular method of cleaning. Then read the ____4____ beside the machine, which explain the sequence of buttons to press. Similar-looking controls do not necessarily work in the same way.

The amount a machine is designed to hold is its ____5____. Packing in more than that amount is not a useful way to save money. Leave enough room for clothes to move, and use an appropriate quantity of detergent. More soap does not automatically produce cleaner clothes.

You may need to ____6____ items that require different treatment, rather than putting everything into one wash. A fabric that tolerates heat well may share a basket with something that does not. The result of ignoring that difference can be permanent ____7____.

When the cycle ends, return promptly to ____8____ your clothes. An occupied machine may look busy even when it has finished, leaving another resident unsure whether it can be used. Check the room's arrangements for items left behind rather than assuming you may leave yours there indefinitely.

Cleaning filters and reporting faults ____9____ can keep a communal service working. A machine is truly ____10____ to the next person only when it is both free and ready for use. Doing laundry is an ordinary task, but sharing the equipment makes small acts of consideration particularly visible.

originalGroup.material:
Finding time for a rehearsal

A student orchestra needed a rehearsal schedule that could accommodate both the performers and the rooms they used. The organiser initially treated each player's free hours as an independent preference. In practice, the relevant ____1____ were connected: a percussionist might be free while the only room large enough for the instruments was not.

The first task was to identify what was ____2____. A rehearsal of the full orchestra required particular players, suitable space and access to the instruments. Other arrangements were more ____3____. A section could sometimes practise separately, and a short discussion about interpretation did not necessarily require the largest hall.

The organiser proposed several ____4____ rather than circulating one supposedly ideal timetable. Musicians could then explain which difficulties each proposal created. This made the ____5____ involved more visible: gaining an extra hour in the large hall might require some players to alter an existing commitment.

Fairness did not mean giving every player an identical schedule. Their roles and practical needs were not identical. It did mean making the reasons for each ____6____ clear, so an inconvenient decision was not mistaken for simple neglect.

After discussion, the group reached a ____7____ that nobody considered perfect but everyone could use. They also built in a small ____8____ between sessions. Without that spare time, one late finish would delay the next group's preparation.

The resulting plan was ____9____ to change if a room became unavailable. Its purpose was coordination, not prediction of a flawless term. Keeping that distinction ____10____ helped the orchestra respond to problems without treating every adjustment as evidence that planning had failed. A useful schedule represented an agreement about how to proceed, together with a way to reconsider it.

originalGroup.material:
The unopened envelope

The ____1____ (DISCOVER) of an unopened envelope behind a drawer led to an ____2____ (EXPECT) visit. I did not recognise the name on the front. Out of ____3____ (CURIOUS), I asked my aunt whether she recognised it.

She explained that the envelope belonged to the previous occupant of the house. There was no ____4____ (PERSON) connection between the writer and our family. We therefore left it sealed while she contacted the former resident through the letting agent.

When he came to collect it, he opened it himself and invited us to look at the card inside. He unfolded it ____5____ (CARE), taking time not to tear its delicate paper edges. It contained a drawing his sister had made as a child, not the formal document I had imagined.

The ____6____ (REAL) that such a small object could matter so much changed my view of it. Its ____7____ (ORIGIN) owner saw a family memory where I had seen a puzzle. Finding something did not give me a right to settle every question about it. His visit revealed a ____8____ (POSSIBLE) I had not considered: a forgotten object could mean far more to its owner than to the finder.
